section.title: Length and area for parametric curves
section.p: The last section used the coordinate rates
to find slope and concavity. Those same rates also measure something more physical: how much distance the moving point travels.
A parametric curve is drawn by motion. So its length should come from speed.

exercise.title: Why is parametric arc length an integral of speed?

statement.p: During a short time \Delta t, the moving point travels about \sqrt{(\Delta x)^2+(\Delta y)^2}. In your own words, why does accumulating those small distances produce \int_a^b\sqrt{(x')^2+(y')^2}\,dt, and why is the graph formula a special case of the same idea?

hint.p: Speed is the Pythagorean combination of the coordinate rates. A graph y=f(x) is the parametrization x=t, y=f(t).

statement.p: If a parametrization traces the same geometric curve twice, the speed integral doubles. In your own words, why is that the right answer for distance traveled and the wrong answer if you wanted the length of the set of points, and what happens if the point pauses for an instant?

hint.p: The integral counts the motion. A zero-speed instant contributes no length; a second tracing contributes a second copy of the length.

statement.p: Area under a graph becomes \int y(t)x'(t)\,dt after the change of variable dx=x'(t)\,dt. In your own words, why can tracing a closed curve clockwise versus counterclockwise change the signed area, and why can repeated tracing double the integral?

hint.p: The formula counts with the parametrization. Direction can reverse the sign; tracing twice can double the count.

warning.title: Warning about repeated tracing
warning.p: The area formulas count with the parametrization.
If a curve is traced twice counterclockwise, the signed area integral doubles. If one part is traced clockwise and another counterclockwise, cancellation can occur.
Before using a closed-curve area formula, check how many times the curve is traced and in which direction.

The point on the wheel momentarily stops when it touches the ground. The curve has cusps there. This is exactly the kind of behavior that parametric equations handle naturally: the formulas describe not only the curve, but also the motion that creates it.

The next coordinate system also comes from motion, but of a different kind. Instead of following horizontal and vertical coordinates, we measure a point by how far it is from the origin and which direction it lies.

exercise.title: What do cycloids show that a static curve equation would hide?

statement.p: A cycloid is traced by a point on a rolling wheel. In your own words, why is a parametrization the natural language for that curve, and what does a cusp at the ground contact reveal about motion versus shape?

hint.p: The formulas describe not only the curve but the rolling that creates it. At a cusp the point momentarily stops, which parametric derivatives detect directly.
